body:
## Summary

Five related bodies of work, grouped so the aggressive cross-application validation happens once:

1. **HTTP serving performance** — ≈ +27–30% on keep-alive workloads vs main, with zero functional loss, no new dependencies, no XS.
2. **CI** (new — this repo had none): GitHub Actions matrix over perl 5.18/5.26/5.32/5.40 × full/bare optional deps, macOS, and a system-perl `ubuntu-24.04-arm` slow-smoker canary with `PERL_TEST_TIME_OUT_FACTOR=3`. The bare profile exercises every optional-dep skip path that has produced CPAN smoker FAILs before.
3. **Outbound byte accounting** — `buffered_amount` and every backpressure/drain check are now O(1) reads of a connection-maintained counter (single `_stream_write` chokepoint + one shared `on_write` callback), eliminating the dependency on IO::Async::Stream's undocumented `writequeue` internals.
4. **header_timeout (slowloris defense)** — a request head must arrive in full within 30s of its first byte (`--header-timeout`, 0 disables; default ON) or the server answers 408 and closes. Total-elapsed semantics, so byte trickling cannot reset it the way it resets the activity-based idle/stall timers; covers the h2c preface wait; enforced by one lazy per-server sweep so the hot path pays a single timestamp store. Part of hardening PAGI-Server for proxyless exposure.

5. **Accept batching (`PAGI::Server::Listener`)** - cleartext listeners drain up to 64 pending accepts per loop iteration instead of stock IO::Async::Listener's one-per-iteration (measured ~32 accepts/sec on a busy worker). Field A/B with hey -c 500 against one worker: slowest request 10.75s -> 0.30s, +3.5% throughput - the connection-storm tail is gone. TLS listeners keep the stock class (the SSL listen extension owns their acceptor). Residual storm bound is kernel queue capacity: somaxconn + --reuseport, documented in Changes.

## Performance (interleaved A/B medians, `bench/run.sh`, single worker, hey c=32, 3×10s)

| scenario | main | branch | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET 13B keep-alive | 3920 | ~5000 | **≈ +27%** |
| POST 1KB echo | 3440 | ~4560 | **≈ +33%** |
| GET 64KB | 1936 | 3000 | **≈ +55%** (autoflush +46%, byte accounting +9%) |
| GET 64KB, degenerate 8KB high-watermark | — | — | −1.9% (per-writer `on_write` disables writer coalescing; only manifests under permanent backpressure) |

Mechanisms, in impact order: inline write flushing (`autoflush`, saving one event-loop cycle per response), 64KB read/write lengths, synchronous fast-path send dispatch, package-level receive/send implementations, single-pass header analysis, serializer-emitted Date, O(1) buffer accounting.

## Bugs the new CI caught (fixed here)

- **Deferred `on_drain` dropped after teardown**: the armed drain fire held the transport handle weakly; under inline flushing a fast client completes the stream before the `loop->later` tick and delivery silently no-ops (deterministic on Linux, bisected in an ubuntu:24.04 container). `TransportState` now captures the callback list strongly; red-green `t/53`.
- **Blocking-handle carp**: `Connection->start` forces handles non-blocking — autoflush on a blocking handle could stall the loop (t/http2/03 hands in a blocking socketpair).
- **t/45 multi-listener flake**: forked clients were only served during a fixed 1s loop window (dead loop once `waitpid` blocks); the parent now serves until the child is reaped, deadline factor-scaled as a hang guard only.

## Verification

- Suite green locally (113 files / 531 tests; was 110/519 on main — four new test files added, no existing test modified except the t/45 timing hardening described above).
- Full 8-job matrix green on the final commit, first attempt.
- Transport subset verified in an ubuntu:24.04 container (202 tests) — the environment that exposed the drain race.
- `t/54` proves the byte counter equals a live walk of the real write queue at every tick under forced backlog, and returns to exactly zero after drain.
- Watermark semantics pinned: writes that would cross the high mark take the deferred path so `pagi.transport` callbacks observe the crossing exactly as before (`t/52`).
- `Changes` carries the full 0.002007 stanza; `bench/` ships in the repo but is pruned from the CPAN dist.

Known-good fallback points if aggressive app testing implicates a layer: `e233163` (everything except byte accounting), `51e2ef7` (pre test-hardening).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

churn. Writes that would reach the high-water mark take the deferred path
so the pagi.transport watermark callbacks still observe the crossing
(_write_app_data); the drain cycle restores inline flushing.

echo 3903.78 (+7.5%), big 2655.12 (+27.7%).

precomputed at parse time. Neutral on the 3-header hey benchmark
(interleaved A/B: 4538 vs 4513 hello r/s, within noise; echo +1%),

The send path no longer copies the response header array on the common
path just to append the date pair; header-name validation runs a single
[[:cntrl:]] match on the good path (same messages, same precedence); the
default-Server-header probe skips the per-header lc() unless the name

commits.messageHeadline: perf: reuse transport-state closures per connection; time requests on…

commits.messageBody:
One compiled body each, shared by every request, instead of building and
tearing down closure CVs per request (and per $receive->() call); the
connection is re-weakened inside the impl so GC timing is unchanged.
Per-request state moves to small state hashrefs.

bench (median r/s): hello 4870.43 (+3.1%), echo 4496.16 (+10.2%).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
commits.messageHeadline: perf: hoist receive/send implementations to package-level async subs

commits.messageBody:
response.start, unthrottled body chunks, trailers, and fullflush never
await, so $send->() now runs them synchronously and returns an immediate
Future instead of spinning up the async-sub state machine per call; the
eval preserves the pre-await-die-becomes-failed-Future contract. Body
writes share one _emit_body_chunk; backpressure and file/fh streaming
delegate to the async _send_body_slow.

bench (median r/s): hello 5056.46 (+3.8%), echo 4586.77, big 2864.42.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
commits.messageHeadline: perf: dispatch non-suspending send events in a plain sub

commits.messageBody:
…atermark checks

Review hardening: suspension (_suspend_autoflush) and restoration
(_on_write_queue_empty, installed once at stream setup) now pair through
one flag instead of coupling four subs, so any future write path that
suspends inline flushing is guaranteed to get it back when the queue
empties. Previously restoration depended on the notify -> arm_drain ->
waiter chain (reachable in all current flows, but silently fragile).
Below-mark writes skip _notify_transport_write: the post-write queue
cannot exceed the pre-write estimate, so the check cannot fire. Adds
t/52-autoflush-restore.t pinning the restore invariant.

the single-scan dispatch (their semantics live in the scan and its
comment); keeping them invited silent divergence. _should_keep_alive now
extracts the first Connection header and delegates to _keep_alive_for so
the keep-alive policy has one implementation. Comment cleanups from
review.

Two axes match this dist's CPAN-smoker failure history: a bare-deps
profile exercises every optional-dep skip path, and a system-perl
ubuntu-24.04-arm job with PERL_TEST_TIME_OUT_FACTOR=3 canaries the

commits.messageHeadline: ci: GitHub Actions matrix — perl 5.18-5.40, full/bare optional deps, …

commits.messageBody:
…ndles non-blocking

CI's Linux jobs caught both. (1) The deferred drain fire held the
transport handle weakly; with inline write flushing a fast client can
complete the whole stream before the loop->later tick, so the armed
on_drain was silently dropped (h2 hit it deterministically on Linux —
reproduced and bisected in an ubuntu:24.04 container; latent race on
main, deterministic regression with autoflush). The fire now captures
the callback list strongly; only the hysteresis reset needs the handle.
Red-green: t/53-transport-drain-after-teardown.t. (2) start() now forces
the handle non-blocking: autoflush on a blocking handle could stall the
loop, and t/http2/03 hands Connection a blocking socketpair (the
O_NONBLOCK carp on Linux full-dep jobs).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
commits.messageHeadline: fix: deliver armed on_drain callbacks after handle teardown; force ha…

commits.messageBody:
…ACTOR

The forked clients are only served while the parent's loop runs its fixed
1s window (waitpid then blocks the loop); a slow shared CI runner can
spawn the child too late and the request is never answered — observed as
a macos-latest flake. Same idiom as the zombie-master deadline fix.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
commits.messageHeadline: fix(test): scale multi-listener serve windows by PERL_TEST_TIME_OUT_F…

commits.messageBody:
A fixed serve window strands a slow child: once waitpid blocks, the loop
is dead and a late request is never answered (hit twice on CI under -j4,
different platforms; 0/60 reproducible under plain CPU stress — the
window design, not the server, is the flaw). The parent now runs the
loop until the child exits, with the factor-scaled deadline kept only as
a hang guard. t/18, t/43, and t/signal-graceful-restart share the old
pattern if they ever flake.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
commits.messageHeadline: fix(test): serve forked multi-listener clients until reaped

commits.messageBody:
… introspection

All connection writes now enter the stream through _stream_write, which
counts bytes out and back in via one shared on_write callback per
connection. buffered_amount and every backpressure/drain check read a
plain integer; the walk of IO::Async::Stream's undocumented writequeue
internals is gone (the invariant test keeps a copy of the walk to prove
the counter exact: t/54).

bench (interleaved pre/post, medians): hello within noise (~-1.6%,
run spread larger), echo neutral-to-positive, 64KB responses +9.0%
(2751.8 -> 3000.1 r/s); degenerate 8KB-high-watermark config -1.9%
(per-writer on_write disables queue coalescing, which only matters
under permanent backpressure). Suite green locally (113 files/531
tests) and in an ubuntu:24.04 container (transport subset, 202 tests).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
commits.messageHeadline: perf: first-class outbound byte accounting; drop IO::Async writequeue…

commits.messageBody:
… defense)

A request head must arrive in full within header_timeout seconds of its
first byte (default 30, --header-timeout, 0 disables) or the server
answers 408 Request Timeout and closes. Total-elapsed semantics: byte
trickling cannot reset it the way it resets the activity-based idle and
stall timers. Also covers the h2c preface wait. Enforced by one lazy
per-server periodic sweep; the hot path pays a single timestamp store
(hello bench unchanged, median 4850 r/s within the session's noise
band). Suite 114 files / 536 tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

IO::Async::Listener accepts one connection per readiness event, capping a
busy process's accept rate at its loop iteration rate (~32/sec measured at
~5k req/s); a 500-connection storm pinned the somaxconn-clamped kernel
queue, dropped SYNs into retransmit backoff, and smeared first-request
latency to 10+ seconds. The subclass drains up to 64 accepts per event
(bounded for fairness to established connections), preserving the parent's
on_accept_error dispatch for real failures (EMFILE) while treating EAGAIN
as queue-drained. Selected only for cleartext listeners: the SSL listen
extension injects its own acceptor, which the subclass bypasses — the
class choice keys off the same _build_ssl_config result that decides the
extension (an earlier tls_enabled-based gate read the flag before it was
set and hung t/08-tls.t; caught by the suite, fixed by hoisting the ssl
decision above the class pick). Field A/B (hey -z 30s -c 500, one worker):
slowest 10.75s -> 0.30s, 5011 -> 5185 req/s. t/00-load.t inventory gains
this module and the previously missing TransportState.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
